newsitem.title: PERU: Peru relatives honor hostages as 5th month starts.
newsitem.headline: Peru relatives honor hostages as 5th month starts.

text.p: Relatives of 72 hostages held by Marxist guerrillas attended an emotional Mass on Thursday to mark the start of the fifth month of the crisis and afterwards released dozens of balloons and a single white dove to mark their call for a peaceful resolution.
The mass was held at a Roman Catholic church close to the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence.

A three-man guarantors commission continued at the same time its hectic but hush-hush shuttle diplomacy between President Alberto Fujimori's government and the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels.

Although there was no official word on Thursday's talks, a Bolivian diplomat struck a rare note of optimism by saying that a solution could come within weeks if the negotiations go on at their present pace.

"We think that within the next 15-20 days there will be a solution," acting Bolivian ambassador Eloy Avila told reporters after the mass. "With the talks continuing so actively it means that they are progressing."
Bolivia's ambassador, Jorge Gumucio, is one of the hostages who have spent more than 17 weeks in cramped conditions in the residence under the gun of roughly 20 jungle-trained rebels.

Roman Catholic Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani and Canadian Ambassador Anthony Vincent, the Vatican and Canadian members of the commission, held talks with MRTA leaders at the residence. They met for two hours and left without comment.
A few blocks away, scores of people left the mass wearing white ribbons and clutching the balloons and walked in a line up to police guarding the compound where their loved ones are held.
To loud applause, they set free the balloons, which drifted in the wind towards the mansion stormed by heavily-armed rebels during a cocktail party on Dec. 17.
Relatives said they were confident the talks would bring a bloodless solution to the crisis -- the worst faced by Fujimori in his seven turbulent years in office.
"We are very convinced this will be resolved in a peaceful way," said Lucia de Gutierrez, whose son-in-law is among the hostages. "Peace is the only way to save lives; anything else is very risky."

The main sticking point remains the MRTA demand for the release of hundreds of jailed comrades. President Alberto Fujimori has publicly ruled this out although sources close to the talks suggest the government may be prepared to free some lesser MRTA prisoners to avoid bloodshed.

Fujimori has already arranged asylum for the 20-odd rebels in Cuba in the event of a peaceful solution, and Cuban Foreign Minister Roberto Robaina reiterated in Tokyo on Thursday that Havana would do "whatever it can" to speed a solution.
